title: Typing Promises and async Code
summary: A Promise type describes the value a waiting job is expected to give back later.
introduction: A Promise type describes the value a waiting job is expected to give back later. Think of a ticket that promises one kind of result. Read the result type, then see how await gives your code that result.
learningObjectives: Declare async functions with Promise<T> return types and read awaited values with the right type
Recognise the compiler errors for a missing await and for using an unknown caught error
Validate a fetch response at runtime instead of asserting its type

blocks.text: `Promise<T>` is a generic type: `T` is what the promise eventually resolves to. An `async` function always returns a promise, so its declared return type is `Promise<User>`, not `User`, even though the body simply returns an object. `await` does the reverse: applied to a `Promise<User>` it produces a `User`. Top-level `await` is allowed in ES modules with a `target` of es2017 or later.

blocks.title: basics.ts
npx tsc basics.ts
blocks.content:
basics.ts:19:21 - error TS2339: Property 'name' does not exist on type 'Promise<User>'.

19 console.log(pending.name);
                       ~~~~

  basics.ts:19:21
    19 console.log(pending.name);
                           ~~~~
    Did you forget to use 'await'?


Found 1 error in basics.ts:19

blocks.text: The first part prints `user-1`. The second part is the classic bug: without `await`, `pending` is a `Promise<User>`, which has `then` and `catch` but no `name`. Plain JavaScript would print `undefined`; the compiler names the problem and even suggests the fix. `wait` shows the manual way to build a promise: the `Promise<void>` annotation lets the compiler check that `resolve` is called with nothing.

A forgotten `await` inside an `if` is nastier, because a promise object is always truthy and the branch always runs. Since TypeScript 4.x the compiler reports a promise used as a condition, and the message again asks the right question.

blocks.title: forgot-await.ts
npx tsc forgot-await.ts
blocks.content:
forgot-await.ts:6:7 - error TS2801: This condition will always return true since this 'Promise<boolean>' is always defined.

6   if (isAdmin(2)) {
        ~~~~~~~~~~

  forgot-await.ts:6:7
    6   if (isAdmin(2)) {
            ~~~~~~~~~~
    Did you forget to use 'await'?


Found 1 error in forgot-await.ts:6

blocks.text: Run the file with `tsx` and it prints `admin` for user 2, which is exactly the security bug the compiler just prevented. The fix is `if (await isAdmin(2))`.

`Promise.all` takes an array of promises and resolves to a tuple of their results in the same order, each with its own type, so destructuring gives `user` a `User` and `count` a `number`. The utility type `Awaited<T>` unwraps a promise type in type position; combined with `ReturnType` it recovers the resolved type of any async function without repeating it.

blocks.title: all.ts

blocks.text: JavaScript lets you `throw` anything, so TypeScript cannot know what lands in a `catch`. Under `strict` (specifically `useUnknownInCatchVariables`) the caught value is `unknown`, and reading `.message` from it is an error until you prove it is an `Error`.

blocks.title: catch.ts
npx tsc catch.ts
blocks.content:
catch.ts:8:15 - error TS18046: 'error' is of type 'unknown'.

8   console.log(error.message);
                ~~~~~


Found 1 error in catch.ts:8

blocks.title: catch-fixed.ts

blocks.text: `fetch` is typed in both the browser and `@types/node`, but `response.json()` returns `Promise<any>`, because nobody can know what a server sends. Assign the result to `unknown`, then prove its shape with a type predicate before returning it as a `Todo`. The predicate is ordinary code that runs at runtime, which is the only kind of check that can protect you from a changed API.

blocks.title: fetch.ts
npx tsc fetch.ts
blocks.content: (no output: the file compiles without errors)

blocks.title: Common mistake: return (await response.json()) as Todo
blocks.text: The cast compiles, looks typed and checks nothing. When the API renames `title` to `name`, every consumer of `getTodo` still believes it has a `title`, and the failure appears far away as `undefined` in the UI. Because `json()` returns `any`, even the cast is optional: `return response.json()` compiles too. Always route external data through `unknown` and a runtime check; for larger shapes use a schema library (such as zod or valibot) that generates both the check and the type.

blocks.title: Where the types come from
blocks.text: `Promise`, `fetch`, `Response` and `setTimeout` are declared in the built-in `lib` files and in `@types/node`, which the [declaration files lesson](/tutorials/typescript/declaration-files) explains. If `fetch` is reported as unknown, check that `@types/node` is installed or that `"lib"` includes `"dom"`.

questions.question: What is the inferred return type of `async function load() { return 42; }`?
questions.explanation: An async function always wraps its return value in a promise, so the return type is Promise<number>.

questions.question: Under strict mode the variable in `catch (error)` has the type `Error`.
questions.explanation: Anything can be thrown, so strict mode types the caught value as unknown. Use instanceof Error to narrow it.

seo.title: Typing async Code in TypeScript – Promise<T>, await, catch
seo.description: Type Promises and async functions in TypeScript, catch forgotten awaits at compile time, handle unknown errors in catch blocks and validate fetch responses.
